desc:
A terrain is a row of unit-width columns; column i is heights[i] units tall. After heavy rain, the water standing above column i is

water[i] = min(L, R) - heights[i]
L = max(heights[0..i]),  R = max(heights[i..n-1])

(the water level over a column is limited by the lower of the tallest column on its left and the tallest on its right, each counting the column itself). A column is wet when water[i] > 0.

Return how many columns are wet. Example: for [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] the wet columns are 2, 4, 5, 6 and 9, so the answer is 5.
hints: Write down when min(L, R) - heights[i] is positive. Remember that L and R both include heights[i] itself.
A column is wet exactly when there is a column strictly taller than it somewhere on its left and somewhere on its right.
Scan once from the left keeping the running maximum to mark columns that have a strictly taller column on the left, then scan from the right the same way, and count columns marked by both passes.
editorial: Because L and R include the column itself, both are at least heights[i]. So min(L, R) > heights[i] holds exactly when L > heights[i] and R > heights[i], that is, when the tallest column strictly before i is taller than heights[i] and the tallest column strictly after i is also taller. Equal-height neighbours do not hold any water in this rule.

Make one pass from the left recording whether the maximum so far exceeds the current column, one pass from the right doing the same, and count the columns where both are true. The same information comes from a monotonic stack that keeps a non-increasing sequence of heights, but the running maxima are simpler and use O(n) time and O(n) space for the marks (or O(1) extra space with a suffix-maximum array reused). This predicate is the first step towards the full trapped-water computations.
